title: Users and password hashing
goal: Store users safely: never plain-text passwords, always a slow salted hash.

concepts: Authentication (who are you?) vs authorisation (what may you do?)
Why plain-text or fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) are wrong for passwords
bcrypt: salt + cost factor; hash on signup, compare on login
A users table: unique lower-cased email, password_hash, created_at
Never return password_hash from the API
Generic login errors ('Invalid email or password') to avoid user enumeration

build.task: In api-starter, add migration 003_users.sql (users: id uuid, email text unique, name, password_hash, created_at) and add user_id to projects (FK, CASCADE). Build a users feature: POST /api/auth/register validates email, name and password (min 8 chars, at least one letter and one number), lower-cases and trims email, hashes with bcrypt (cost 12), returns 201 with { id, email, name } and never the hash. Duplicate email returns 409. Add a script scripts/hash-timing.ts that times bcrypt at cost 10, 12 and 14 and records the results in docs/passwords.md with your explanation of why slow is good.
acceptance: Passwords stored only as bcrypt hashes (check in psql)
Email normalised; duplicate (even with different case) returns 409
Password rules enforced by zod with clear messages
Response and logs never contain password or hash
docs/passwords.md has the timing results and explanation

hints: import bcrypt from 'bcrypt'; const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12); later: const ok = await bcrypt.compare(password, user.password_hash);
Catch the unique violation: if (e.code === '23505') throw new ConflictError('Email already registered'). Or check first, but the constraint is what really prevents races.
Select only safe columns in your repo: RETURNING id, email, name, created_at.
proof: Commit with the migration, auth register route and docs/passwords.md.

explainBack.q: Why is bcrypt better than SHA-256 for passwords?
lookFor: SHA-256 is designed to be fast

explainBack.q: What is a salt and what attack does it stop?
lookFor: stops cracking many users at once

lastHintExplanation: Fast hashes like SHA-256 let an attacker with a stolen database try billions of guesses per second. bcrypt is deliberately slow, and its cost factor lets you make it slower as hardware improves. Each hash includes a random salt, so two users with the same password get different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables are useless.

predict.q: bcrypt.hash('secret123', 12) is called twice. Are the two hashes equal?
options: No, each has a different random salt
Only if cost is the same
predict.why: A new salt is generated each time; compare() still verifies both.

title: Login with JWT
goal: Issue a signed JSON Web Token on login and understand exactly what's inside it.

concepts: Sessions (server stores state) vs tokens (client holds a signed token)
JWT structure: header.payload.signature (base64url, NOT encrypted)
Signing with a secret (HS256); verifying detects tampering
Claims: sub (user id), iat, exp; keep the payload small and non-secret
Short-lived access tokens; the trade-offs of refresh tokens
Where to store tokens on the client: memory/localStorage vs httpOnly cookies

resources.title: jwt.io: Introduction to JSON Web Tokens
OWASP: JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet

build.task: In api-starter: npm i jsonwebtoken (and -D @types/jsonwebtoken). Add JWT_SECRET (min 32 chars, validated) and JWT_EXPIRES_IN (default '1h') to config. POST /api/auth/login: find the user by lower-cased email, bcrypt.compare, and on success return { token, user: { id, email, name } }; on any failure return 401 'Invalid email or password' (same message and similar timing for unknown email and wrong password). Paste a real token into jwt.io and write docs/jwt.md explaining each part, why anyone can read the payload, and what happens if you change one character of the payload.
acceptance: Login returns a signed token with sub and exp claims
JWT_SECRET is validated at startup and never committed
Unknown email and wrong password give the same 401 response
No sensitive data (password, hash, email if you can avoid it) in the token payload
docs/jwt.md decodes a real token and explains tampering

hints: jwt.sign({ sub: user.id }, config.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: config.JWT_EXPIRES_IN }) returns the token string.
Same timing: if the user isn't found, still run bcrypt.compare against a fixed dummy hash so both paths take about as long.
proof: Commit with the login route and docs/jwt.md.

explainBack.q: Anyone can decode a JWT payload. So what stops a user from changing sub to someone else's id?
lookFor: signature computed with the server secret

explainBack.q: Why return the same error for 'unknown email' and 'wrong password'?
lookFor: attacker can't learn which emails are registered

lastHintExplanation: A JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone can base64-decode the payload, but the signature is an HMAC of header and payload made with the server's secret. Change one character and verification fails, and without the secret nobody can forge a new valid signature. Identical errors for unknown emails and wrong passwords stop attackers discovering which emails have accounts.

predict.q: A JWT has exp set to one hour after issue. The server restarts after 10 minutes with the same secret. Is the token still valid?
options: Yes, the server holds no state; it just verifies the signature and exp
predict.why: JWTs are stateless; verification needs only the secret and the clock.

title: Protecting routes and per-user data
goal: Require a valid token on private routes and make sure users can only see and change their own data.

concepts: Authorization: Bearer <token> header
requireAuth middleware: verify, attach req.user (or res.locals.user), 401 on failure
401 (not logged in) vs 403 (logged in but not allowed) vs 404 (hide existence)
Scoping every query by user_id: WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2
IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): the most common API security bug
GET /api/auth/me for the current user

resources.title: OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken Object Level Authorization

build.task: In api-starter: write requireAuth middleware (reads Bearer token, jwt.verify, sets res.locals.userId, returns 401 with your error format for missing, invalid or expired tokens). Protect all /api/projects and /api/tasks routes and add GET /api/auth/me. Update every repo method to take userId and scope its SQL by it (projects by user_id; tasks via their project's user_id). Create two users, A and B, and prove in docs/authz-tests.md (curl commands + outputs) that B cannot list, read, update or delete A's projects or tasks, and that such attempts return 404.
acceptance: Requests without or with a bad/expired token return 401
Every project and task query is scoped by the current user
User B gets 404 for every operation on user A's data (documented)
GET /api/auth/me returns the current user without the hash
No route trusts a user id sent in the body or query

hints: const header = req.get('authorization'); if (!header?.startsWith('Bearer ')) return next(new UnauthorizedError()); try { const p = jwt.verify(header.slice(7), config.JWT_SECRET); res.locals.userId = p.sub; next(); } catch { next(new UnauthorizedError()); }
Tasks belong to users through projects: UPDATE tasks t SET ... FROM projects p WHERE t.id = $1 AND t.project_id = p.id AND p.user_id = $2 RETURNING t.*
Returning 404 rather than 403 for other users' objects avoids revealing that the id exists.
proof: Commit with requireAuth, scoped repos and docs/authz-tests.md.

explainBack.q: What is IDOR? Show how your API would have been vulnerable without user_id scoping.
lookFor: changing an id in the URL accesses another user's data
token proves identity but not ownership
fixed by WHERE user_id = current user

explainBack.q: When do you return 401 vs 403 vs 404?
lookFor: 404: to hide existence of others' resources

lastHintExplanation: A valid token proves who the user is, not that they own the object in the URL. Without scoping, user B could change /tasks/<id> to one of A's ids and read or delete it. That's IDOR, the most common API vulnerability. Putting AND user_id = $2 in every query makes ownership part of the lookup, so other users' rows simply aren't found (404).

predict.q: requireAuth is applied with app.use('/api/projects', requireAuth, projectsRouter). Is /api/auth/login protected?
predict.why: The middleware only runs for paths under /api/projects.

title: Auth in Angular: login, interceptor and guards
goal: Add sign-up, login and logout to your Angular app, with the token attached automatically and private pages guarded.

concepts: An AuthService holding the token and current user in signals
Persisting the token (localStorage) and restoring it on startup with /auth/me
An auth interceptor adding Authorization: Bearer ...
Handling 401 globally: log out and redirect to /login?returnUrl=...
A canActivate guard for private routes
XSS risk with localStorage tokens, and httpOnly cookies as the alternative

build.task: In your task-manager Angular app: add /register and /login pages (reactive forms with server error messages shown), an AuthService (token and user signals, login, register, logout, restoreSession calling /api/auth/me on startup), an authInterceptor adding the Bearer header to /api requests, an error interceptor that on 401 logs out and navigates to /login?returnUrl=<current>, and an authGuard on all project pages. Show the user's name and a logout button in the header. After login, return to returnUrl. Write docs/token-storage.md comparing localStorage and httpOnly cookies.
acceptance: Register, login and logout all work against your API
Reloading the page keeps you logged in (session restored via /auth/me)
Private pages redirect to login when logged out, then return to the original page
An expired or invalid token logs you out cleanly on the next request
docs/token-storage.md explains the XSS and CSRF trade-offs

hints: Guard: export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = (route, state) => inject(AuthService).isLoggedIn() ? true : inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login'], { queryParams: { returnUrl: state.url } });
Don't add the token to requests to other domains: only if req.url.startsWith('/api') or your API base URL.
Test expiry quickly by setting JWT_EXPIRES_IN=30s on the server.
proof: Commit with auth pages, service, interceptors and guard.

explainBack.q: Is the Angular guard a security measure? Explain.
lookFor: real protection is the API's requireAuth and scoping

explainBack.q: What's the main risk of storing a JWT in localStorage, and what's the trade-off with cookies?
lookFor: any XSS script can read localStorage
httpOnly cookies can't be read by JS

lastHintExplanation: Route guards only control what the Angular app shows. Anyone can call the API directly, so real security lives on the server (requireAuth plus user scoping). A token in localStorage can be stolen by any injected script (XSS). An httpOnly cookie can't be read by JavaScript, but browsers send it automatically, so you then need CSRF protection such as SameSite cookies.

predict.q: The interceptor adds the token to every request, including https://openlibrary.org. What's the problem?
options: Your token is leaked to a third party
predict.why: Only attach credentials to your own API.

title: Hardening the API
goal: Apply the standard security basics every production Express API should have.

concepts: helmet: secure HTTP headers
Rate limiting login and register to slow brute force
Body size limits (express.json({ limit: '100kb' }))
Secrets only in env; rotating a leaked secret
Logging without sensitive data (passwords, tokens)
npm audit and keeping dependencies updated
OWASP Top 10 at a glance

build.task: In api-starter: add helmet, a 100 kb JSON body limit, and express-rate-limit on /api/auth/* (e.g. 10 requests per 15 minutes per IP, returning your error format with 429). Make the logger redact authorization headers and any password fields. Disable the X-Powered-By header (helmet does this). Run npm audit and fix what you can. Write docs/security-checklist.md going through each OWASP API Top 10 item: does it apply, and what you did (or would do) about it. Prove the rate limit with a loop of 12 curl login attempts and paste the output.
acceptance: helmet headers visible in curl -i output
11th auth request within the window gets 429 in your error format
Bodies over 100 kb get 413
Logs never contain tokens or passwords (show a sample)
npm audit has no high or critical issues (or each is explained)
docs/security-checklist.md covers all 10 OWASP API items

hints: import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'; const authLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60_000, limit: 10, standardHeaders: 'draft-7', legacyHeaders: false, handler: (req, res) => res.status(429).json({ error: { code: 'RATE_LIMITED', message: 'Too many attempts, try again later' } }) });
Behind a proxy like Coolify or Nginx, set app.set('trust proxy', 1) so the limiter sees real client IPs instead of the proxy's.

Curl loop (bash): for i in $(seq 1 12); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST localhost:4000/api/auth/login -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"email":"a@b.c","password":"wrongpass1"}'; done
proof: Commit with the hardening changes and docs/security-checklist.md.

explainBack.q: What does rate limiting the login route protect against, and what are its limits?
A teammate accidentally commits JWT_SECRET to GitHub. What do you do?
lookFor: removing from git history isn't enough

lastHintExplanation: Rate limiting makes brute-forcing passwords from one IP impractically slow, but attackers with many IPs can still spread attempts, so it's one layer among several. A leaked secret must be rotated at once: deleting the commit doesn't help because clones, forks and caches may already have it. Rotating also logs everyone out, which is the point.

predict.q: The API runs behind a reverse proxy without trust proxy set. What does the rate limiter see as every client's IP?
options: The proxy's IP, so everyone shares one limit
predict.why: Without trust proxy, req.ip is the proxy's address.

title: Debug lab: the leaky auth middleware, and week review
goal: Find authentication and authorisation bugs that would let users in, or see others' data.

concepts: jwt.decode does NOT verify; always use jwt.verify
Leaking password hashes through SELECT *
Missing ownership checks (IDOR)
Wrong status codes for auth failures
Reading security code with an attacker's mindset

build.task: Copy the starter into day108-debug/ in node-playground, npm install, npm start. Use curl: log in as asha@example.com / password123 and as ravi@example.com / password456. Expected: a token with a tampered payload (edit it on jwt.io without the secret) gets 401; GET /me never contains passwordHash; Ravi gets 404 for GET /notes/1 (Asha's note); no Authorization header gets 401 (not 500). There are 4 bugs. Write the attack that proves each bug before fixing it, and fix each in its own commit. Write week18-notes.md (Days 103–107).

starterFiles.name: day108-debug/server.js

acceptance: Tampered or forged tokens get 401 (jwt.verify used)
/me returns only id, email and name
Users get 404 for other users' notes
A missing or malformed Authorization header gets 401, not 500
4 fix commits, each with the attack written in the commit message; week18-notes.md written

hints: Take Ravi's token, change sub from 2 to 1 on jwt.io (the signature will be wrong), and call /me. Whose data comes back? Which function checks the signature, and which only reads the payload?
Look at everything /me returns. Should a client ever see that field?
Ravi asks for /notes/1. Nothing compares note.userId to req.userId. And with no header at all, req.headers.authorization is undefined, so .split crashes, which the error handler turns into a 500.
proof: Link to your last fix commit.

explainBack.q: List the 4 bugs, the attack for each and the fix.
lookFor: no ownership check on notes → IDOR → filter by userId
missing header crashes → 401 check before split

explainBack.q: Why is jwt.decode dangerous in auth middleware?

lastHintExplanation: 1) jwt.decode only base64-decodes the payload, so anyone can forge sub: 1 and become Asha; jwt.verify checks the signature. 2) /me returns the whole user object, including passwordHash; return only safe fields. 3) /notes/:id never checks ownership (IDOR); require note.userId === req.userId and return 404 otherwise. 4) A missing header makes .split throw, giving a 500; check for 'Bearer ' first and return 401.
